title: Arguments & Validity
description: Premises, conclusions, and what makes reasoning work

concepts.title: What is an Argument?
concepts.contentHtml:
In philosophy, an argument is not a quarrel — it's a structured attempt to support a claim.

Every argument has two parts: premises (the reasons offered) and a conclusion (the claim those reasons support).

Example:

P1: All humans are mortal.
P2: Socrates is human.
∴ Socrates is mortal.

The symbol ∴ means 'therefore'. The conclusion follows from the premises.

concepts.title: Validity vs Soundness
concepts.contentHtml:
An argument is valid if the conclusion must be true whenever the premises are true. Validity is about structure, not truth.

An argument is sound if it is valid and all its premises are actually true.

'All cats can fly. Whiskers is a cat. So Whiskers can fly' is valid (the form works) but not sound (premise 1 is false).

Validity is necessary but not sufficient for a good argument.

concepts.title: Deductive vs Inductive
concepts.contentHtml:
Deductive arguments aim for certainty: if the premises are true, the conclusion must be true. Math proofs are deductive.

Inductive arguments aim for probability: the premises make the conclusion likely, but not guaranteed. 'Every swan I've seen is white, so all swans are white' is inductive — and famously turned out wrong when black swans were discovered in Australia.

Science mostly runs on induction; logic and math run on deduction.

title: Common Fallacies
description: Reasoning errors that fool even careful thinkers

concepts.title: Ad Hominem & Strawman
concepts.contentHtml:
An ad hominem attacks the person instead of their argument. 'You can't trust her economic theory — she's been divorced twice!' Her marriages are irrelevant to her economics.

A strawman distorts an opponent's position into a weaker version, then attacks that. 'You support a carbon tax? So you want everyone to ride bicycles to work in the snow!'

Both fail because they don't engage with what was actually said.

concepts.title: Appeals to Authority & Tradition
concepts.contentHtml:
Appeal to authority: 'Einstein believed in God, so God exists.' Einstein was a physicist, not a theologian — his expertise doesn't transfer.

Citing a real expert in their field is fine. Citing them outside their expertise is the fallacy.

Appeal to tradition: 'We've always done it this way, so it must be right.' Slavery, bloodletting, and flat-earth cosmology all had tradition on their side.

Age of an idea is not evidence of truth.

concepts.title: Slippery Slope & Circular Reasoning
concepts.contentHtml:
Slippery slope: 'If we allow X, then Y will happen, then Z, then catastrophe!' — without showing each step is actually likely.

Sometimes slopes really are slippery; the fallacy is asserting it without evidence.

Circular reasoning (begging the question): the conclusion is hidden inside the premises. 'The Bible is true because the Bible says so.' The argument assumes what it tries to prove.

Spotting circularity: ask 'what would convince me this is wrong?' If nothing could, you may be in a circle.

title: Formal Logic & Truth Tables
description: Symbols, connectives, and the algebra of true/false

concepts.title: Propositions and Connectives
concepts.contentHtml:
A proposition is a statement that is either true or false — never both, never neither. 'Paris is in France' is a proposition. 'Close the door!' is not.

Propositions can be combined using logical connectives:

— AND (∧): both must be true
— OR (∨): at least one true
— NOT (¬): flips the value
— IF...THEN (→): false only when antecedent is true and consequent false

This abstraction lets us reason without worrying about specific content.

concepts.title: Truth Tables
concepts.contentHtml:
A truth table lists every combination of input truth values and the resulting output.

For P ∧ Q (AND), only TT gives T; everything else gives F.

For P ∨ Q (OR), only FF gives F; everything else gives T.

For P → Q, the only false case is T→F (a true premise leading to a false conclusion would falsify the implication).

Truth tables turn logical reasoning into mechanical computation — you can verify any complex formula by brute force.

concepts.title: Logical Equivalence and De Morgan's Laws
concepts.contentHtml:
Two formulas are logically equivalent if they have the same truth table — they say the same thing in different forms.

De Morgan's Laws are the most useful equivalences:

¬(P ∧ Q) ≡ ¬P ∨ ¬Q
¬(P ∨ Q) ≡ ¬P ∧ ¬Q

In English: 'not both' equals 'either not'. 'Not either' equals 'neither'.

These laws power Boolean simplification — and your computer's circuits run on exactly this algebra.

concepts.title: From Propositions to Predicates
concepts.contentHtml:
Propositional logic treats whole sentences as atoms. Predicate logic looks inside.

A predicate is a property or relation that takes one or more arguments: M(x) for 'x is mortal', L(x, y) for 'x loves y'.

This lets us express patterns propositional logic can't reach. 'Socrates is mortal' becomes M(Socrates). And we can talk about all the other things that might or might not be mortal.

This expressive jump is why predicate logic is the workhorse of mathematics and philosophy.

concepts.title: Quantifiers — ∀ and ∃
concepts.contentHtml:
Predicate logic adds two quantifiers:

∀ (universal) — 'for all'. ∀x P(x) means every x has property P.
∃ (existential) — 'there exists'. ∃x P(x) means at least one x has property P.

Quantifiers negate via De Morgan: ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x). 'Not everyone is happy' = 'someone is unhappy'.

Order matters: ∀x ∃y L(x,y) ('everyone loves someone') is very different from ∃y ∀x L(x,y) ('someone is loved by everyone').

concepts.title: Translating Natural Language
concepts.contentHtml:
Natural language often hides logical structure. Translating helps you see what's really claimed.

'Every cat is a mammal' → ∀x (Cat(x) → Mammal(x))
'Some birds can't fly' → ∃x (Bird(x) ∧ ¬Fly(x))
'No fish is a mammal' → ∀x (Fish(x) → ¬Mammal(x))

Watch the connectives. Universal claims pair with → (if it's a cat, then it's a mammal). Existential claims pair with ∧ (it's a bird AND it can't fly).

Mixing these up is the most common mistake in formal translation.

title: Famous Paradoxes
description: When logic seems to break itself

concepts.title: The Liar Paradox
concepts.contentHtml:
'This sentence is false.'

If it's true, then what it says is the case — it's false. If it's false, then what it says isn't the case — so it's true. Either way, contradiction.

The Liar shows that self-reference plus truth predicates can break naive language.

Tarski's response: forbid a language from talking about its own truth. Object-language sentences are evaluated in a meta-language. Build levels — and the paradox disappears because no sentence can refer to its own truth-status.

concepts.title: The Sorites (Heap) Paradox
concepts.contentHtml:
A million grains of sand is a heap. Remove one — still a heap. Remove another — still a heap. Repeat. By induction, one grain is a heap. By another iteration, zero grains is a heap.

The puzzle: vague predicates ('heap', 'tall', 'bald') resist sharp boundaries, but logic seems to demand them.

Responses include fuzzy logic (truth values between 0 and 1), epistemicism (there IS a sharp line, we just don't know it), and supervaluationism. No consensus — vagueness remains philosophically alive.

concepts.title: Russell's Paradox
concepts.contentHtml:
Consider the set R of all sets that don't contain themselves. Does R contain itself?

If R contains itself, then by definition (it doesn't contain itself) it doesn't. If R doesn't contain itself, then by definition it does. Contradiction.

Bertrand Russell discovered this in 1901, undermining Frege's foundational system for mathematics. The fix was axiomatic set theory (ZFC) — restrictive rules about how sets can be formed, blocking the construction of R.

This paradox transformed logic and the foundations of mathematics in the 20th century.
